Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

1 · Generate, then select

Creativity needs both exploration and systematic evaluation — schedule both, never in the same minute.

The first stage is to make the map. The second stage is to choose a route on the map.

(de Bono 1985, 199)

Image: Concept-art sheet from the short film Sprite Fright: seventeen labelled versions of one red-haired character's head, each with a different expression.

Sprite Fright concept art: Victoria · Julien Kaspar / Blender Foundation · CC BY 4.0 · Source

  • Generation and selection are two different jobs. Doing them in the same minute makes both weaker.
  • That is why the Lab runs them as two exercises: silent brainwriting first, selection second.
  • Honest audit: was your last piece one first idea polished, or one of several considered on purpose?
  • Some briefs really do need the first answer. When time is the constraint, generate-then-select is a luxury.
  • Judging too early has a cost: students who expected their artwork to be evaluated produced work judged less creative.
  • One small lab study: open-monitoring meditation helped a divergent-thinking task.

Source: the map/route quote is (de Bono 1985, 199); one creative act holds both divergent and convergent thinking is (Craft 2000, 30); the evaluation result is (Amabile 1979, 221); the meditation study is (Colzato, Ozturk, and Hommel 2012, 1). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Where does the line fall between "take the first answer" and "generate more"?

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

2 · Fluency with flexibility

Many ideas only help if they differ. Thirty sketches of the same sun are many ideas, but only one kind.

It involves fluency, or the ability to generate a great quantity of ideas; flexibility, or the ability to switch from one perspective to another; and originality in picking unusual associations of ideas.

(Csikszentmihalyi 1996, chap. 3)

Course diagram · Koch triangle · #5cc4358a9bdb · Original course SVG

  • In the Lab you count both: how many ideas (fluency) and how many kinds (flexibility).
  • Someone has to decide whether two passages are different possibilities or variations of one.
  • Selection follows the period of production; it does not interrupt it.

Source: the slide quote is (Csikszentmihalyi 1996, chap. 3); "Lateral thinking is generative. Vertical thinking is selective." is (de Bono 1970, introduction). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: How do you decide if two ideas are different, or one idea twice?

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

3 · Get past the obvious

Your first ideas are often the obvious ones. In this Lab, don't censor them — keep making more without judging, and dig in a different place.

You cannot dig a hole in a different place by digging the same hole deeper.

(de Bono 1970, introduction)

Image: A wall covered with columns of handwritten blue and orange sticky notes from a brainstorming session, each note a separate idea kept without judging.

Stickies to brainstorm · Victor Grigas · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Source

  • First ideas are often the obvious ones, and they are sticky: designers tend to "hang on to their principal solution concept", and a fixation effect, suggested by Jansson and Smith, makes designers shown an example copy its features.
  • "Generate numerous ideas. It is dangerous to become fixated upon one or two ideas too early in the process."
  • Osborn's first rule: "Criticism must be withheld until all ideas are in."
  • In this Lab: produce more without judging instead of censoring; brainwrite in silence, then come back in Exercise 2 as a selector. On your D1, count how many ideas you wrote before one felt neither obvious nor random.

Source: the dig-hole quote is (de Bono 1970, introduction); stickiness and fixation are (Cross 2006, 81–82); "Generate numerous ideas…" is (Norman 2013, 226); the rule is (Osborn 1942, chap. 4); looking for alternatives instead of accepting the most obvious approach is (de Bono 1970, chap. “The Generation of Alternatives”). The Lab bullet is course wording.

Ask: How many ideas are enough for a given brief? The lesson leaves this open.

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

4 · Role and constraint tools

Hats and cards stage a cognitive move — map the kinds of thinking first, then choose a route.

Any tool should be useful in the expected way, but a truly great tool lends itself to uses you never expected.

(Raymond 2001, 44)

Image: A workshop board headed 'Sombrero negro (Dudas)' — the black thinking hat — asking 'What are the doubts? What are the risks?', with coloured sticky-note answers below.

Sombrero negro (Dudas) · NMontoya (WMCO) · CC BY 4.0 · Source

  • The studio is never neutral: the first voice can narrow the room. Role and constraint tools disturb that frame.
  • Six Thinking Hats: one mode at a time. White facts, red feelings, black caution, yellow benefits, green new ideas, blue running the process.
  • An Oblique Strategies card gives one short prompt for changing a D1 object. It is a deck of prompts, not a theory or a guarantee.
  • de Bono: lateral thinking is provocative, "a way of bringing about repatterning". What-if thinking widens the alternatives you consider, but it can hurt the generation of new ideas.

Source: the tool quote is (Raymond 2001, 44); provocation and repatterning are (de Bono 1970, chap. “Difference between Lateral and Vertical Thinking”); what-if thinking is (Wong, Galinsky, and Kray 2009, 161, 168). The Hats and Oblique Strategies bullets are course wording (the lesson names the hats without a page cite).

Ask: Who speaks first in your group, and what does that close?

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

5 · Name selection criteria

Convergent choice needs explicit novelty and fitness-to-brief tests — name your criteria before you rank.

Editing is a demonstration of taste. It isn't expressed through pointing to items we like… Our taste is revealed in how our work is curated.

(Rubin 2023, 386)

Image: A Pugh concept-selection spreadsheet: criteria such as reliability and safety with weights in rows, four design concepts scored in columns, and totals at the bottom.

Pugh Concept Selection · Chattons2 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Source

  • Unstated criteria favour whatever the room already leaned toward.
  • Name the criterion before you decide what to keep. The scoring is the design act, not the ranking.
  • Editing as taste revealed in curation is selection criteria by another name, not a substitute for writing them down.
  • Selection is the neglected half: creativity is usually defined by production, not by how ideas are evaluated and dismissed.

Source: editing as "a demonstration of taste" revealed in curation is (Rubin 2023, 386); creativity "usually defined in terms of the production end" with evaluation and selection neglected is (Persaud 2007, 68). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Whose criteria decide what counts as "novel"?

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

6 · Workshops are means, not genius

Fluency training supports practice; landmark ideas are rare — workshops train the hand, not replace genius myths.

Artists are often portrayed in films and books as tortured geniuses. Starving, self-destructive, dancing on the brink of madness.

(Rubin 2023, 323)

Image: Van Gogh's 1889 self-portrait: the painter in a cap and green coat, a white bandage wrapped around his head, with a Japanese print on the wall behind him.

Self-portrait with bandaged ear · Vincent van Gogh · Public domain · Source

  • Brainwriting produces material you did not have in view. That does not mean the exercise produced better ideas.
  • Fluency, flexibility and originality are what most tests measure and most workshops train. Workshops try to raise those scores.
  • Landmark work is rare, depends on its system, and cannot be produced on command in a two-hour block.
  • The only practice that matters is the one you keep doing; test any method on yourself instead of copying it.

Source: the slide quote on artists portrayed as tortured geniuses is (Rubin 2023, 323); the lesson's point on practice is (Rubin 2023, 326); the test dimensions and "most workshops try to enhance" are (Csikszentmihalyi 1996, chap. 3). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Which idea on your brainwriting sheets could become evidence for D1, and what criterion would justify that choice?

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

Exercise 1 · 6-3-5 brainwriting against solo writers

Write three ideas, pass your sheet to the left, and build on what you read. Three silent rounds, shortened from six. Some teams work alone instead — then compare the counts.

Practises Masterclass 1–3: generate first, count kinds as well as ideas, get past the obvious.

Save your sheet or solo list, your team’s two counts and the class comparison.

Image: Black-and-white photograph of the Zen teacher Kōdō Sawaki seated cross-legged in robes, upright and still, hands resting in his lap in meditation.

Kodo Sawaki, zazen · Unknown photographer (c. 1920) · Rights under review · Source

  • Timer: one 4-minute round (restart it for each round). Whole exercise about 20 minutes.
  • Optional warm-up, 3 minutes: sit comfortably and notice thoughts, sounds or sensations without holding on to any. Anyone may opt out: sit quietly, read the brief, or start early. No posture or breathing instructions.
  • Split the class: brainwriting teams of six (3–6 works) and solo teams of the same size, all on the same brief.
  • Brainwriting: three ideas per row, one per column; pass left; read, then write three new or built-on ideas. Silent.
  • Shortened: a team of six needs six rounds (about 30 minutes) to pass every sheet to everyone; we run 3 rounds and say so.
  • Solo teams: each person writes alone for the same 12 minutes; lists are pooled only at the end.
  • Each team removes repeats and counts different ideas (fluency) and different kinds (flexibility). Compare on the board. Keep the sheets for Exercise 2.

Source: the warm-up rests on one small lab study in which open-monitoring meditation helped a divergent-thinking task (Colzato, Ozturk, and Hommel 2012, 1); that study used sessions of about 35 minutes, so the 3-minute version is untested. 6-3-5 and the solo comparison are a classroom adaptation in course wording.

Ask: Which kind of team had more ideas, and more kinds? What did passing sheets do to yours?

Creativity Techniques · U2 Idea Generation and Selection

Exercise 2 · Select: hits, COCD box, yellow and black hats

Choose in three steps: dot the strongest ideas, sort them in a now / wow / how grid, then test your top three with the yellow hat, then the black hat.

Practises Masterclass 4–5: role tools, and naming your selection criteria.

Save the dots, the grid, the yellow and black notes, and the criterion behind your pick.

Course diagram · Koch triangle · #5cc4358a9bdb · Original course SVG

  • Timer: 20 minutes — about 5 for hits, 7 for the grid, 8 for the hats. Same teams as Exercise 1.
  • Hits: all sheets up. In silence, each person dots the ideas or parts that look strong. No discussion yet.
  • Take the ideas with the most dots (around ten) to a 2×2 grid: how new (low/high) against how feasible (low/high).
  • Name the corners: now (feasible, ordinary), wow (feasible and original), how (original, not yet feasible); drop the fourth. Keep the wow ideas; pick a top three.
  • Yellow hat, 3 minutes: everyone thinks only about why each idea could work. Black hat, 3 minutes: only about why it could fail.
  • Decide: one idea, one written criterion. Then compare: is your pick also the idea the team rated most original? If not, why?

Source: silent dot stickers on the strongest parts (a heat map) are (Knapp, Zeratsky, and Kowitz 2016, chap. 10); the yellow hat covering hope and positive thinking and the black hat covering why it cannot be done are (de Bono 1985, 32). The COCD box, the step order and the comparison question are course wording.

Ask: Did the criterion you wrote down match the reason you actually chose?

Carry forward

No Workshop in first lessons — Lab ends the session. D1 Analysis does not get Workshop time. From session 4: half Transposition, half final event.

Whose criteria decide what counts as novel — yours, the brief's, or the room's?

(Tao of Creativity)
